chapter_title: North, South, East, West (Dreams and Discoveries)
subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.activity_title: Postcards from India: A First Meeting with Shaana

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.118): paired discussion on a memorable travel experience.

homework.task_brief: Let us read (p.118): fill in six details about your own State or Union Territory.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick paired exchange: ask students to tell their partner one place they have enjoyed visiting, who they went with, and one thing they learned. Take two or three brief whole-class sharings to warm up the room.

Introduce Shaana and the postcard format. Read the first two or three postcards aloud, with students following in their textbooks (p.118–122), pausing to model how a reader notices a new geographical detail or a moment of surprise in Shaana's voice.

Continue reading aloud through postcards covering Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, and Arunachal Pradesh (p.122–125). Invite students to share aloud one image or detail that struck them — snowballs at Thajiwas, the treehouse forest walk — and briefly discuss what kind of land each place seems to be.

Close by asking students to name two geographical features Shaana has encountered so far, noting these on the board. Explain the homework task and ensure every student has located p.118 in the textbook before they leave.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening reading establishes Shaana's chatty, warm postcard voice; encourage students to notice her personality as well as the geography. A common difficulty is treating every postcard as equally weighted — steer attention toward details that reveal both landscape and character. Students who have not done the homework task can still participate fully because all textual work in this unit begins and ends here.
materials: Class textbook — North, South, East, West (p.118–125)
Board or chart for noting geographical features

periods.activity_title: Wetlands, Deserts, and the Journey South

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.125): complete the places-and-descriptions table from Shaana's postcards.

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the remaining postcards — Sundarbans, Gujarat, Goa, Chennai, Puducherry, and Rameswaram (p.125–124) — with students following in their textbooks. Pause briefly at each new landscape so students can note the terrain type: wetland, desert, plateau, coast.

Distribute or display the 'Places Visited / Interesting Descriptions and Activities' table from p.125. In pairs, students work through the rows for Himachal Pradesh, the treehouse forest, Gujarat, the Narmada, Chennai, and Olaikaadu, locating evidence in the postcards. Circulate and prompt with questions such as 'What did Shaana hear at night in Himachal?' or 'How does she describe floating at Olaikaadu?'

Take whole-class feedback row by row; build a shared version of the table on the board. Highlight two or three moments where Shaana's language itself signals wonder or nervousness — for example, 'I hope they don't follow us home' — so students see how description and emotion are woven together.
Briefly ask: which place in the table would you most want to visit and why? Take two or three quick responses to close.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the postcards covering glaciers, forests, wetlands, deserts, plateaus, and coastlines, students now organise that content systematically. Watch for students who fill in only the most obvious details — prompt them to look for Shaana's own words as evidence rather than general knowledge. No prior table or homework is needed; the text itself is the resource.
materials: Class textbook — North, South, East, West (p.125–127)
Board for building shared table

periods.activity_title: Reading the Postcards Closely: Wonder, Fear, and Change

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.126): extract questions on the Sundarbans postcard — inference and evidence.
Let us think and reflect (p.126–127): extract questions on the night-train plateau postcard — attitude change.

homework.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.127): answer any two of the extended questions on India's geography and Shaana's language.

time_bands.activity: Ask students to re-read silently the Sundarbans postcard extract printed at the top of p.126 ('Amma tells me…'). Give them a moment to mark any word or phrase that signals a feeling.

Work through the Let us think and reflect questions on Extract 1 (p.126) as a guided whole-class discussion: ask students to choose the MCQ option and justify it aloud, complete the fill-in blank with a reason drawn from the text, identify the phrase that signals nervousness, and evaluate the assertion–reason pair. Accept divergent readings and press for textual evidence each time.

Move to Extract 2 (p.126–127, the night-train postcard). Students work in pairs on the fill-in and the MCQ about Shaana's attitude change toward tunnels; then discuss in whole class. Draw attention to the phrase 'I used to be afraid… but I'm not any more' as an example of how Shaana communicates personal growth in a chatty register.

Close with a brief whole-class reflection: what two things do Shaana's observations about less snow and more flooding tell us about the environment? Take two or three responses and acknowledge the climate-change thread running through the postcards. Set the homework task.

periods.teacher_notes: Having built a panoramic picture of Shaana's journey through the places-and-descriptions table, students now read two extracts with precision. A common difficulty is answering 'how does the speaker feel?' with a general word rather than a textual phrase — consistently return students to the words on the page. The extended questions on p.127 are set as homework; any two are sufficient, giving students a genuine choice.
materials: Class textbook — North, South, East, West (p.126–127)
Board for recording textual evidence

periods.activity_title: Listening to the Story of Agartala and Agarwood

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.131–132): listen to the Agartala passage and choose the correct option for five questions.

time_bands.activity: Ask students: 'Do you know the meaning of any Indian city's name?' Take a few responses to activate curiosity. Tell students they are about to hear a short talk about how a North-East Indian capital got its name and why the tree behind that name is remarkable.
Display or read aloud the five questions from p.131–132 so students know what to listen for. Ask them to keep their textbooks closed during the listening.

Read the Agartala transcript aloud at a measured pace — this is the full talk about 'agar' and 'tala', agarwood's scent, its ancient uses, how it forms when the tree is infected, and its importance in Tripura today. Read it a second time; students may make brief notes on each question as they listen.

Students mark their chosen options. Go through each question in whole-class discussion, asking students to justify their choice with a detail they heard. Correct any mis-hearings by re-reading the relevant sentence from the transcript.

periods.teacher_notes: Having journeyed across India through Shaana's postcards, students now encounter the North-East through an oral talk — a different register and mode. Watch for students who open their textbooks during listening; the purpose of closed-book listening is to develop auditory retention. If the room is noisy, a second reading of the whole passage before question discussion is appropriate.
materials: Class textbook — North, South, East, West (p.131–132)
Listening transcript (p.138) — teacher copy

periods.activity_title: Travel Preferences: Comparing and Expressing Choices

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.132–133): share and compare travel preferences in pairs using the given sentence starters.

time_bands.activity: Read the seven preference questions from p.132–133 aloud with the class: bus or train, family trip or school trip, beaches or mountains, and so on. Ask students to tick their own preference for each question privately before pairing up.

Display the sentence frames on the board: 'I prefer… to… because…', 'I would rather… than… because…', 'I am alright with both, but I prefer… because…', and the remaining frames from p.133. Model one complete exchange with a volunteer, demonstrating how to use a frame to give a reason.

Students work in pairs, moving through all seven questions and responding using the sentence frames. Circulate to encourage students who use only one frame to try another, and to help any students who slip into their home language when reasoning.

Invite three or four pairs to share one contrast from their conversation with the whole class — choosing a preference on which they disagreed. After each sharing, ask the class: did anyone have the same contrast? This surfaces how diverse preferences can coexist, connecting gently to the chapter's theme of India's diversity.

periods.teacher_notes: Having listened to a talk and answered questions in the previous unit, students now shift to producing language themselves. A common difficulty is students stating a preference without a reason — the sentence frames are designed to force the reasoning clause, so insist on its use. Students who are quieter in whole-class settings often participate more confidently in pairs; allow adequate pair time before whole-class sharing.
materials: Class textbook — North, South, East, West (p.132–133)
Board for displaying sentence frames

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.133): draft a formal leave application to the Principal using the given format and verbal cues.

time_bands.activity: Ask students: 'If you needed a few days off school for a family event, how would you ask the Principal?' Take two or three informal responses. Then display or read the application format from p.133 — address block, date, recipient line, subject line, salutation, body, closing — naming each part and its purpose.

Model one short leave application on the board, thinking aloud as you write: choosing how many days, naming the event, framing the promise to complete school work. Point out register markers — 'I respectfully request', 'Yours sincerely' — that distinguish a formal application from informal writing.

Students write their own application independently, using the format and verbal cues on p.133. Circulate and offer brief individual prompts: 'Have you named your class, section, and roll number?', 'Is your reason specific enough?' Encourage students to read each sentence aloud softly to check it sounds formal.

Students exchange drafts with a partner for a paired peer-read: the partner checks one thing — whether the subject line clearly names the number of days and reason. Two or three volunteers read their opening body paragraph aloud, and the class notes one formal phrase used well.

periods.teacher_notes: Having practised oral comparison of preferences, students now shift to formal written register — a significant gear change. The most common error at this stage is a subject line that is vague ('Request for leave') rather than specific ('Request for leave for three days to attend a family event'). Peer review in the closing minutes gives students a light revision loop before they finalise their drafts, so the entire writing cycle — plan, draft, respond — completes within this unit.
materials: Class textbook — North, South, East, West (p.133)
Board for modelled application
Lined writing paper or notebooks

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.129): match context-clue situations to six words from the text.
Let us learn (p.130): underline subjects and verbs in sentences drawn from the postcards.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.131): choose the correct verb form in ten subject–verb agreement sentences.

time_bands.activity: Display the six situations from p.129 one at a time — for example, 'heard a loud noise in the night and felt afraid' — and ask students which word from the box (blink, scary, existed, amazing, splashed, floating) fits. After students respond, confirm by locating each word in the postcards text, showing that context in the story reveals meaning.

Introduce subject–verb agreement using the three sentences from p.130: 'Amma and Appa are fast asleep', 'It's hot, dry, and there is sand everywhere', and 'There are so many hills here, and beaches too.' Work through each sentence together: students identify the subject, state whether it is singular or plural, and underline the matching verb. Discuss the rule for compound subjects joined by 'and' and for sentences opening with 'there'.

Quick practice: call out two or three additional travel-themed sentences — 'A pair of binoculars _____ useful on safari', 'Either the guide or the tourists _____ to arrive first' — and invite hands-up responses with a brief justification. Set the ten-sentence homework task from p.131.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit focuses on vocabulary drawn directly from Shaana's postcards and on the grammar of subject–verb agreement as it appears in sentences from the text. A frequent confusion is the 'there is / there are' inversion: students apply the rule for compound subjects and miss that the grammatical subject follows the verb in those sentences. Keep returning to the actual postcard sentences as anchor examples.
materials: Class textbook — North, South, East, West (p.128–131)
Board for sentence analysis

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.131): choose the correct verb form (is/are, was/were, etc.) in ten subject–verb agreement sentences.

time_bands.activity: Briefly revisit the rules practised in the context of Shaana's postcards: compound subject + 'and' takes a plural verb; 'either…or' and 'neither…nor' agree with the subject closer to the verb; 'a pair of', collective nouns like 'information' and 'news' take singular verbs. Write two or three trigger phrases on the board as anchors.

Students work through the ten sentences on p.131 individually, selecting the correct verb form and noting the rule that governs each choice. After ten minutes, pair students to compare and reconcile any disagreements before whole-class feedback begins.

Go through each sentence in whole-class discussion, asking students to state the rule aloud before confirming the answer. Pay extra attention to sentences 2 ('Either…or'), 4 ('Neither…nor'), and 8 ('Keeping accounts') where errors are most likely.
Close with a brief self-correction check: students mark any sentence they got wrong and write the correct rule beside it in their notebooks, creating a personal reference.

periods.teacher_notes: Having introduced subject–verb agreement rules through the postcard sentences, students now apply those rules across a variety of sentence structures. The 'either…or / neither…nor' proximity rule is the hardest for most students at this stage — devote extra whole-class time to sentences 2 and 4. No homework artefact from the previous unit is required; the exercise on p.131 is self-contained and marked here.
materials: Class textbook — North, South, East, West (p.131)
Board for rule reminders

periods.activity_title: India's Landmarks: Crossword, Research, and Local Discovery

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore (p.134): solve the India landmarks crossword using State and Union Territory clues.
Let us explore (p.135): research and share a unique heritage place from your own village, region, or state.

time_bands.activity: Students work individually or in pairs on the crossword puzzle from p.134, using the landmark clues — Pangong Lake, Thar Desert, Gangotri Glacier, Hampi, and others — to identify States and Union Territories. After ten minutes, allow students to cross-check with a neighbour and fill any remaining blanks collaboratively.

Introduce the local heritage task from p.135, using the Ellora Kailasa temple and Rani-ki-Vav examples to show the kind of detail expected: location, what makes it unique, and its historical or cultural significance. Students spend this time writing a short paragraph (four to six sentences) about a place they know from their own village, region, or state — drawing on personal knowledge or any available reference material in the room.

Three or four volunteers share their place with the class in a quick round — one sentence on location, one on why it is remarkable. Record the place names on the board to build a class map of local heritage knowledge.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked through the full text, language exercises, and writing task, students now extend the chapter's theme of India's diversity outward — from the textbook's examples to their own communities. Some students may be uncertain what counts as 'unique'; assure them that a local water body, craft tradition, or festival is as valid as a UNESCO site. The paragraph begun here is complete within this unit and does not require continuation.
materials: Class textbook — North, South, East, West (p.134–135)
Board for recording place names
Any available reference material — atlas, library books, or teacher-supplied notes

periods.activity_title: Synthesis: Shaana's Journey and India's Story

time_bands.activity: Open with a whole-class recollection: ask students to name one geographical feature per region of India that appears in Shaana's postcards — glaciers in Kashmir, mangroves in the Sundarbans, desert in Gujarat, plateaus in Goa, beaches in Puducherry. Write the features on the board under North, East, West, and South to reconstruct the journey spatially.

Pose three integrating questions for small-group discussion: How does Shaana's voice change from the early postcards to the final one addressed to her parents? What do her references to less snow and more flooding add to a travel account aimed at classmates? Which geographical region surprised you most, and why? Groups share a key insight with the whole class.

Students write a short reflective response — six to eight sentences — comparing two regions Shaana describes, drawing on any geographical, environmental, or personal detail from the postcards. The comparison should name at least one specific feature of each region and one thing Shaana says or does in each place. This is completed within the unit.

Close with a read-aloud of Shaana's final postcard addressed to Amma and Appa — a tender note of gratitude for glaciers, forests, deserts, wetlands, plateaus, and mountains. Ask one final question: what does it mean to travel not just through places but through the chapter of a country's geography? Take two or three responses and let those close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis unit draws on the entire chapter — Shaana's postcards, the agarwood listening text, the speaking preferences, the leave application, vocabulary from the postcards, and the India landmarks exploration — as content already familiar to students, regardless of which particular activities their class completed. The comparison writing begins and ends here; it is not a continuation of any earlier draft. Students who found Shaana's environmental observations (flooding, reduced snow) most striking will have the richest material for both the discussion and the written comparison.
materials: Class textbook — North, South, East, West (p.118–135, full range)
Board for geographical features map
Lined writing paper or notebooks

items.source_lo: Student reads an informational travel text closely to infer feelings, identify evidence for stated observations, and interpret how a chatty personal register conveys both geographical knowledge and emotional growth.
items.source_context: Shaana's postcards: wetlands, glaciers, tunnels, climate observations, Sundarbans flooding, personal growth through travel.
items.item_stem:
In the postcard from the Sundarbans, Shaana writes that she sees crocodiles and a snake while boating, and then says she hopes they do not follow her home. Which of the following best describes the feeling Shaana most likely has when she writes this?
A. deep scientific curiosity about reptiles found in wetlands
B. playful nervousness — acknowledging real wildlife while lightening the mood
C. genuine fear that the animals will actually travel with the family
D. pride in spotting rare wildlife that her classmates have never seen

options.label: A
options.text: deep scientific curiosity about reptiles found in wetlands

options.label: B
options.text: genuine fear that the animals will actually travel with the family

options.label: C
options.text: playful nervousness — acknowledging real wildlife while lightening the mood

options.label: D
options.text: pride in spotting rare wildlife that her classmates have never seen

what_each_option_reveals.A: Suggests the student reads Shaana's tone as factual and informational, missing the humour and personal register of the postcards.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Suggests a literal reading of the joke — the student does not recognise Shaana's characteristic habit of lightening a moment with a funny aside.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Introduces a competitive or boastful motive not present in Shaana's warm, inclusive voice anywhere in the postcards.

items.source_lo: Student reads an informational travel text closely to infer feelings, identify evidence for stated observations, and interpret how a chatty personal register conveys both geographical knowledge and emotional growth.
items.source_context: Shaana's postcards: wetlands, glaciers, tunnels, climate observations, Sundarbans flooding, personal growth through travel.
items.item_stem: In her postcards, Shaana mentions two environmental observations: there is less snow on the glaciers than expected, and the Sundarbans floods far more than it used to. Her mother is described as sad about the flooding, and her father notes that the Narmada's water level is too low for rafting. What do these three observations, taken together, suggest Shaana is beginning to understand about the places she is visiting? Support your answer with evidence from at least two of the three situations described above.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Together the three observations point toward environmental change — reduced glacial snow, increased flooding in the Sundarbans, and a lower water level on the Narmada all signal that natural systems are being disrupted, likely by climate change. Shaana conveys this through her parents' reactions rather than stating it directly, suggesting she is beginning to understand that travel reveals not only India's beauty but also its environmental challenges.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a short informational talk to identify specific factual details and chooses correctly among given options, demonstrating accurate auditory comprehension.
items.source_context: Agartala's etymology, agarwood's formation when infected, scent, ancient uses, importance in Tripura.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the talk about Agartala and agarwood. Then decide whether each of the following statements is True or False.
1. The name 'Agartala' is made up of the words for 'tree' and 'underneath'.
2. Agarwood is described as having a woody and citrusy scent.
3. Agarwood forms when the agar tree is injured or infected by a bug or virus.
4. The agar tree was once nearly extinct but is now found in almost every home in northern Tripura.
5. The Egyptians used agarwood incense more than 5,000 years ago.

options.text: Agarwood forms when the agar tree is injured or infected by a bug or virus.
Agarwood is described as having a woody and citrusy scent.
The agar tree was once nearly extinct but is now found in almost every home in northern Tripura.
The Egyptians used agarwood incense more than 5,000 years ago.
The name 'Agartala' is made up of the words for 'tree' and 'underneath'.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. True — 'agar' means the tree and 'tala' means underneath, so Agartala means 'under the agar tree'.
2. False — the talk describes agarwood's scent as woody and flowery, not woody and citrusy.
3. True — the talk states agarwood forms when the tree is hurt or infected with a bug or virus.
4. True — the talk says the tree was once almost extinct but can now be found in almost every house in northern Tripura.
5. False — the talk states the Egyptians used agarwood incense more than 3,000 years ago, not 5,000.

items.source_lo: Student listens to a short informational talk to identify specific factual details and chooses correctly among given options, demonstrating accurate auditory comprehension.
items.source_context: Agartala's etymology, agarwood's formation when infected, scent, ancient uses, importance in Tripura.
items.item_stem: The talk about agarwood explains that the tree produces a dark, sticky, sweet-smelling substance called agar oil. Why does the tree produce this substance, and what does it tell us about the relationship between the tree's survival and the value humans place on agarwood? Answer in two or three sentences.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The tree produces agar oil as a defence mechanism — when it is hurt or infected by a bug or virus, the oil protects it from further infection rather than allowing it to die. This means the very quality that makes agarwood so valuable to humans — its distinctive scent and the dark resinous wood — is a product of the tree's struggle to survive. The talk thus draws an ironic connection: the tree's wound becomes the source of one of the world's most prized and expensive materials.

items.source_lo: Student uses structured comparison frames in a guided paired conversation to express and justify personal travel preferences clearly and with appropriate reasoning.
items.source_context: Paired comparison of travel preferences — mode, company, destination, activities, season — using sentence frames.
items.item_stem: Shaana travels by different means across India — she crosses the Pamban bridge by train, boats through the Sundarbans, and walks through a forest to reach a treehouse. Think about how you would like to travel on a long journey. Tell your partner: which mode of travel do you prefer — train or bus — and what kind of destination appeals to you more — beaches or mountains? Use at least two of the sentence frames you have practised: 'I prefer… to… because…' or 'I would rather… than… because…' or 'Given a choice, I would go for… over… as…'

expected_elements: States a clear preference for mode of travel with a reason.
States a clear preference for destination type with a reason.
Uses at least two different sentence comparison frames correctly.
Speaks in complete sentences without falling into a list of answers.

items.source_lo: Student uses structured comparison frames in a guided paired conversation to express and justify personal travel preferences clearly and with appropriate reasoning.
items.source_context: Paired comparison of travel preferences — mode, company, destination, activities, season — using sentence frames.
items.item_stem: Shaana's last postcard is addressed to her parents rather than her classmates — she thanks them for sharing glaciers, forests, deserts, wetlands, plateaus, and mountains with her, and wishes she could return with friends someday. Your partner feels that a school trip is always better than a family trip because friends make every experience more exciting. You feel the opposite. Role-play a short conversation in which each of you argues for your view, using evidence from your own experience or from what you know about travel. Use the frames 'I prefer… to… because…' and 'I understand your point, but I think… because…'

expected_elements: Each speaker states and defends a position with at least one reason.
Each speaker acknowledges the other's point before countering.
Uses comparison frames accurately; reasoning is drawn from real or plausible experience.
Conversation has a back-and-forth structure, not two separate monologues.

items.source_lo: Student writes a formal functional document — a leave application — using a prescribed format, appropriate register, and specific content details, demonstrating control of formal written English.
items.source_context: Leave application to school Principal: travel to hometown for family event, duration, reason, plan to complete school work.
items.item_stem: Your cousin's wedding is being held in your hometown next month. You need to take three days off from school. Write a formal application to the Principal of your school requesting leave. Your application must include: the correct format (address, date, recipient designation, subject line, salutation, body, closing); the exact number of days and the reason for the leave; a clear mention of how you will ensure your schoolwork is not affected.

expected_elements: All format parts present: address, date, To the Principal, subject line, salutation, closing.
Subject line names both the number of days and the reason specifically.
Body states reason clearly and commits to completing missed schoolwork.
Formal register throughout — no colloquial phrases or contractions.

items.source_lo: Student writes a formal functional document — a leave application — using a prescribed format, appropriate register, and specific content details, demonstrating control of formal written English.
items.source_context: Leave application to school Principal: travel to hometown for family event, duration, reason, plan to complete school work.
items.item_stem: Shaana, in her postcards, writes warmly and personally to her classmates. Imagine you are Shaana writing the same leave application to her school Principal before her family journey began. Now write that application — requesting leave for the duration of a long family trip across India. You may decide how many days the trip will take. Your application should: follow the correct format; give a clear, specific reason for the leave; include a committed, believable plan for keeping up with schoolwork during the journey; and maintain a formal, respectful tone throughout — even though Shaana's usual voice is chatty and informal.

expected_elements: Full formal format followed correctly with all required parts.
Reason is specific and relates to a family journey across India.
Schoolwork plan is realistic and mentioned explicitly in the body.
Formal register is sustained; contrast with Shaana's chatty postcard voice is evident.

items.source_context: Six context-matched words from the postcards; subject–verb agreement with 'and', 'there', 'either…or', 'neither…nor', pair of, singular nouns.
items.item_stem: Match each word from Shaana's postcards in Column A with the situation in Column B that best shows its meaning.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A (Word)|Column B (Situation)
floating|A leaf drifts slowly on the surface of a still pond without sinking.
wetlands|Low-lying ground near a river where water and land overlap and mangroves grow.
rafting|Travelling down a fast-moving river on an inflated rubber craft.

items.source_lo: Student identifies vocabulary meaning from contextual situations and applies subject–verb agreement rules — including compound subjects, 'either…or', 'neither…nor', and collective nouns — in travel-themed sentences drawn from the text.
items.source_context: Six context-matched words from the postcards; subject–verb agreement with 'and', 'there', 'either…or', 'neither…nor', pair of, singular nouns.
items.item_stem:
Three of the sentences below contain a subject–verb agreement error. Identify each error, write the correct verb form, and name the agreement rule that applies.
1. The information about travel routes are updated every season.
2. Neither the forest trail nor the river path were marked on the map.
3. Amma and Appa was excited to reach the Sundarbans.
4. A pair of binoculars were kept ready for the wildlife watch.
5. There is many glaciers in the northern regions of India.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Sentence 1: 'are' should be 'is' — 'information' is a singular uncountable noun and always takes a singular verb. Sentence 3: 'was' should be 'were' — when two subjects are joined by 'and', the verb is plural. Sentence 5: 'is' should be 'are' — in sentences beginning with 'there', the verb agrees with the subject that follows it, which here is 'many glaciers' (plural). Sentences 2 and 4 are correct: 'neither…nor' agrees with the subject closer to the verb ('path' — singular, so 'was' is correct), and 'a pair of' takes a singular verb ('was').

items.item_stem: The chapter mentions two UNESCO World Heritage Sites as examples of India's ancient places: the Kailasa cave temple at Ellora and Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, Gujarat. Choose a heritage place — a monument, natural feature, festival, craft tradition, or historic site — from your own village, district, or state that you think deserves to be better known. Write a short informational paragraph of six to eight sentences about it. Your paragraph should describe where it is located, what makes it unique or significant, and why you believe others should know about it.

expected_elements: Names a specific, identifiable place, tradition, or feature with its location.
Describes at least one distinctive quality that sets it apart from other places.
Gives a historical, cultural, or environmental reason for its significance.
Concludes with a clear statement of why it deserves wider recognition.
